findings.title: Chi2 primary p reproduces
findings.description: The paper's single inferential result reproduces exactly from the counts it prints. Reconstructing the 2x2 as 3/28 versus 2/28 and running an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared returns p = 0.639339, which rounds to the printed 0.639. The reported statistic is therefore internally consistent with the reported data, and the choice of convention (uncorrected Pearson) is identifiable from the p-value alone. Separately flagged below is whether that convention was the appropriate one.

findings.notes: READ THE ASSUMPTION BEFORE READING THE FLAG. The ceiling of 5.09 is derived from a range of 20 to 30 years, which is MY translation of the phrase 'in their 20s'. The paper prints no age range, no minimum and no maximum, so bound_source is 'assumed' and the tool caps the verdict at 'suspicious' under rulebook rule 4; this cannot be escalated. Both group SDs (5.84 and 6.33) exceed that assumed ceiling, and the SE reading is far worse (implied SDs of 30.9 and 33.5), so neither dispersion interpretation fits a strictly 20-29 cohort. The most likely innocent explanation is simply that 'in their 20s' is loose descriptive prose for a predominantly young cohort rather than an inclusion criterion, and that the sample actually extends into the teens and thirties -- in which case the SDs are unremarkable and nothing is wrong. What is recorded here is the tension between the cohort as described and the dispersion as reported, not an arithmetic impossibility. This must not be presented as a headline finding: the repository's own rulebook cites the phrase 'in their 20s' as a documented route to a false accusation, and the paper's Discussion in fact criticises prior work for a 'wide range of patient's age', which would be self-defeating if its own range were genuinely 20-29. The control-group row (SD 6.33) was checked identically and returned the same verdict.

findings.title: Grim no discriminating power ages
findings.description: GRIM was run on both group mean ages and REFUSED both times, which is the correct outcome and is recorded so it cannot be mistaken for a pass. At n = 28 with one printed decimal every value on the printed grid is attainable as a mean of 28 integers, so the check has no resolution and could not have failed whatever the paper reported. Two further preconditions were also unmet and are worth naming: the paper never states that age was recorded in whole years (it could be a decimal age computed from dates of birth), so discreteness_source is 'assumed'; and the bounds passed are my own translation of 'in their 20s'. No inference about the ages can be drawn from this check in either direction.

findings.title: Beta mislabelled as power (Discussion, sample-size paragraph)
findings.description: A notation error, in a load-bearing sentence: this is the paper's entire justification for its sample size. The conventional reading -- beta = 0.20, hence 80% power -- is almost certainly what the authors did, and under that reading nothing numeric is wrong. But as printed the sentence asserts that the power was 0.20. Recorded because it sits in the sample-size justification rather than in incidental text, and because it cannot be resolved from the paper alone: a reader cannot tell from this sentence whether the authors targeted 80% power and mislabelled the symbol, or targeted something else. No arithmetic is involved, so no tool applies and none is missing.

findings.notes: The paper's headline conclusion is a null claim -- that continued postoperative antibiotics may be unnecessary -- and it rests on a single non-significant p-value with no confidence interval, no risk difference and no effect size anywhere in the paper. absence_of_evidence, the tool for exactly this claim, therefore could not be run: it requires an interval, or a coefficient with a standard error, and the paper prints neither. The only effect estimate recoverable is the odds ratio of 1.56 that recalc_chi_squared returned from the reconstructed 2x2, and no registered tool produces an interval around it from cell counts, so the largest effect the data still permit cannot be quantified here. With 3 and 2 events in arms of 28, that interval would in any case be very wide, and 'not significant' cannot be read as 'no difference'. This is a reporting-practice finding: it describes what the publication omits, and no arithmetic of ours is involved.
findings.reproduction: No runnable command: metascience absence-of-evidence requires --ci-low/--ci-high or --b/--se, and the paper reports no interval and no standard error for its primary comparison.

findings.title: Single test no multiplicity (Whole paper)
findings.description: Recorded as a deliberate decision not to run multiplicity_report. The paper reports exactly one inferential test, on its single stated primary outcome, so there is no family and no correction is owed. findings.title: No blinding or outcome assessor independence (Methods, paragraphs 1 and 2)
findings.description: A design reading, recorded under rulebook rule 5 (does the analysis and conduct match the design). The paper is presented as a prospective randomised study but states that no placebo was given, describes no blinding of patients, surgeon or assessors, and adopts CDC criteria of which the fourth is 'Diagnosis of SSI by the surgeon or attending physician' -- while all operations were performed by the same oral surgeon. Outcome ascertainment was therefore open and partly subjective. The phrase 'did not receive the placebo' uses the definite article for a placebo that is never otherwise mentioned, which reads as residue from an earlier protocol or draft that included one. The paper is presented as a prospective randomised study but states that no placebo was given, describes no blinding of patients, surgeon or assessors, and adopts CDC criteria of which the fourth is 'Diagnosis of SSI by the surgeon or attending physician' -- while all operations were performed by the same oral surgeon.
